caption:
Two inventors just sued Anthropic and OpenAI in Delaware federal court.
Their company, Flinn AI, says each lab infringed five patents on attention-based neural networks, filed in late 2015 and early 2016.
It lands while Anthropic is on its IPO roadshow.

Should anyone be able to patent the tech behind modern AI?

paragraphs.text: Flinn Artificial Intelligence Technologies LLC filed two patent infringement lawsuits in the US District Court for the District of Delaware on November 12, 2026, one against Anthropic PBC and one against OpenAI OpCo, according to Bloomberg Law. Each complaint alleges infringement of five patents.

Reuters described the plaintiff as a company that owns patents invented by a pair of computer scientists. Bloomberg Law identified the co-inventors as Steven Flinn and Naomi Moneypenny and described Flinn AI as an artificial intelligence company founded by a computer scientist.

The patent applications date to late 2015 and early 2016, according to TokenPost and Bloomberg Law. The complaints describe the inventions as neural network technology built around attention, which they say supports important functions in modern generative AI systems. Bloomberg Law reported that the complaints call the applications directed to a new generation of attention-based neural network technology.

The available reports on the filings do not list the patent numbers, the specific products accused or the amount of damages sought. No statements from Anthropic, OpenAI or Flinn AI were included in the coverage.

The suits arrive as Anthropic prepares to go public. On November 10, 2026, Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 per share and launched its IPO roadshow, planning to list Class A shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT, RTTNews reported. The company is offering 801.35 million Class A shares, with another 23.65 million coming from selling stockholders. Seven companies, including AMD, Google, Microsoft and NVIDIA, agreed to buy $26 billion of Class N common stock at the IPO price in a private placement.

It is not the first patent case against Anthropic. In July 2026, the University of Tennessee Research Foundation sued Anthropic in federal court in Delaware over two patents covering neuroscience-inspired neural network methods, accusing Claude Code and its underlying software, TipRanks reported. The foundation sought damages and asked the court to bar Anthropic from using the disputed technology if infringement is found. That suit was described at the time as the first patent infringement case brought against the company. On the day it became public, a California federal judge gave final approval to Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement of a copyright case brought by authors over training data.

Most legal fights over generative AI so far have centered on training data and copyright. Patent claims aimed at the model architecture itself are a different kind of risk, because they target how the systems work rather than what they were trained on. The early filing dates in 2015 and 2016 are likely to be central to how the cases develop.
Watch for the companies' first responses in the Delaware court and for whether Anthropic lists the Flinn suit among the legal risks in its IPO materials.
